voyages.record: First jetliner service with fare-paying passengers

vessel.name: Comet 1 G-ALYP 'Yoke Peter' (BOAC)

facts.Fate: broke up off Elba, 10 Jan 1954 (BOAC Flight 781)

vessel.history: G-ALYP was the first production Comet. On 2 May 1952 it flew the world's first jetliner flight with fare-paying passengers, opening BOAC's London–Johannesburg service.
vessel.story: On 10 January 1954, 20 minutes after leaving Rome Ciampino, G-ALYP broke up in mid-air off Elba with 35 on board. Recovered wreckage showed fatigue cracks from a window corner, and later airliners were designed to be fail-safe.

routes.history: On 2 May 1952 BOAC's de Havilland Comet G-ALYP flew the world's first jetliner flight with fare-paying passengers, opening London–Johannesburg. The five-stop flight was scheduled at 21 h 20 min. By summer 1953 eight BOAC Comets left London each week, three of them for Johannesburg.
routes.story: All Comet 1s were grounded in April 1954 after a series of crashes caused by metal fatigue. The redesigned Comet 4 opened the first transatlantic jet service in October 1958.

vessel.name: Douglas DC-6B (SAS)
vessel.history: SAS became the first airline to fly a scheduled polar route, from Copenhagen to Los Angeles with DC-6Bs, starting on 15 November 1954.
vessel.story: A tariff that allowed free transit via Copenhagen to other European cities made the route popular with American tourists through the 1950s.

routes.history: After pioneering flights in the 1930s and 1940s, SAS made the first commercial polar route crossing: Douglas DC-6B flights between Copenhagen and Los Angeles via Kangerlussuaq (Søndre Strømfjord) and Winnipeg, starting 15 November 1954.
routes.story: Canadian Pacific followed with Vancouver–Amsterdam in 1955, and Pan Am and TWA with West Coast–Paris/London in 1957.

routes.history: In February 1957 SAS was first again, flying Europe to Tokyo over the pole via Anchorage with Douglas DC-7Cs; Air France and KLM followed in 1958. Anchorage stayed a Europe–Japan stop for decades: in 1983 seven airlines flew Japan–western Europe via Anchorage.
routes.story: SAS sold the route as part of a round-the-world service over the North Pole. Most of the 1983 Anchorage flights were early Boeing 747s.

vessel.name: Clipper Victor (Boeing 747-100, Pan Am)
vessel.history: Pan Am's inaugural 747 service was due on the evening of 21 January 1970 with Clipper Young America, but an engine failure delayed it for hours and Clipper Victor was substituted.
vessel.story: Clipper Victor was lost seven years later at Tenerife (1977), when it collided on the runway with a KLM 747-200.

routes.history: The Boeing 747 entered service on 22 January 1970 on Pan Am's New York–London route. Pan Am had asked for a jet two and a half times the size of the 707 to cut seat costs by 30%, and ordered 25 747-100s in April 1966.
routes.story: First Lady Pat Nixon christened Clipper Young America on 15 January 1970, but on inauguration night its engine failed and Clipper Victor flew the first service after a delay of several hours.

vessel.name: Concorde (British Airways)
vessel.history: Concorde began scheduled service with British Airways and Air France on the same day, 21 January 1976. Twenty were built, of which 14 were production aircraft for airlines.
vessel.story: Its only competitor, the Tupolev Tu-144, carried passengers only from November 1977 until a crash in May 1978.

vessel.story: Air France flew its last commercial Concorde flight on 30 May 2003, five months before British Airways retired its fleet.
